vt33_the_schools.topic: What the mystery cults and philosophical schools taught about the soul's ascent (Eleusis, Samothrace, Orphic/Pythagorean, Mithras, Isis, Neoplatonists)

claims.text: Celsus (quoted by Origen, Against Celsus 6.22) described a Mithraic 'ladder with seven gates and, at the top, an eighth gate': lead (Kronos/Saturn), tin (Aphrodite), copper (Zeus), iron (Hermes), mixed metal (Ares), silver (Moon), gold (Sun); Origen rejected the account

Mithraeum of Felicissimus, Ostia (probably second half of 3rd c.): floor mosaic panels pair seven grades with planets: Corax-Mercury, Nymphus-Venus, Miles-Mars, Leo-Jupiter, Perses-Moon, Heliodromus-Sun, Pater-Saturn; inscription FELICISSIMVS EX VOTO F(ecit)

Samothrace: Sanctuary of the Great Gods; anyone without blood guilt could be initiated 'whether enslaved, free, Greek, non-Greek, male, or female'; protection at sea; Diodorus: initiates 'more pious and more just'; Philip II and Olympias initiated there; last securely dated initiate list later 2nd c. CE, cult 'gradually died out' (Wescoat)

About 40 'Orphic' gold tablets, mostly 4th-1st c. BCE, placed in graves; instruct the dead to avoid one spring and drink from the Lake of Memory; formula 'I am the son of Earth and Starry Heaven. But my race is heavenly'; label 'Orphic' a modern invention, none mention Orpheus

Pythagoras espoused metempsychosis, transmigration of the soul into new human or animal bodies; some teachings secret ('not be presented in public to the uninitiated'), many not; akousmatikoi/mathematikoi split (Iamblichus; Zhmud thinks later invention); elusive Orphic-Pythagorean connection
Eleusis participant categories included first-time initiates and those who had attained epopteia, 'who had learned the secrets of the greatest mysteries'
Cicero on Eleusis: the mysteries showed 'how to live joyfully' and taught 'how to die with a better hope'
Porphyry (Life of Plotinus 23): during his six years with Plotinus, Plotinus four times attained union with 'God over all', who 'has neither shape nor form'
Proclus (412-485) headed the Athenian school as diadochos for almost fifty years after Syrianus (d. 437); practised theurgy (Marinus), wrote Hymns and the Elements of Theology (217 propositions)
Plutarch (Alexander 2): Philip was initiated at Samothrace at the same time as Olympias, fell in love with her and was betrothed to her

vt33_the_closings.topic: The closings 391-c.537 by actor and document: Serapeum, Eleusis, Hypatia, temple conversions, Justinian's Athens decree and Philae, Library of Alexandria

claims.text: Socrates HE V.16: at Theophilus's request the emperor ordered Alexandria's temples demolished and put Theophilus in charge; he cleared out the Mithreum and displayed its mysteries publicly, destroyed the Serapeum; violence on both sides; images melted into church vessels for the poor, one statue kept 'lest... the heathens should deny that they had ever worshiped such gods'

Serapeum (391): statue of Serapis struck with an axe by a soldier at Theophilus's instigation, broken up and burned (Rufinus HE XI.23); temple replaced by a martyr's shrine and church; Eunapius describes temples becoming tombs
Eleusis: Theodosius ended pagan sacrifice and cults in 392; sanctuary may have operated some years longer; destroyed by Alaric
Telesterion: religious use ended after Theodosius's decree c.390; Alaric's forces ravaged Attica in 396 'destroying the Telesterion, which was never to be rebuilt'

Eunapius (Lives 475-476), himself initiated, reports the last legitimate hierophant's prophecy; a man from Thespiae, 'a pater in the ritual of Mithras', became hierophant; Alaric entered Greece through Thermopylae in 395; Eunapius blames the impiety of 'men clad in black himatia'

Hypatia killed March 415 in Lent, fourth year of Cyril's episcopate; mob led by 'a reader named Peter' took her to the Caesareum church, killed her with tiles, burned remains at Cinaron; rumour she prevented Orestes' reconciliation with the bishop; brought 'opprobrium... upon Cyril' and the Alexandrian church

Hypatia sources: Socrates does not say Cyril ordered it; Damascius says Cyril envied and plotted; John of Nikiu hostile to her and hails Cyril; Philostorgius blames the Homoousian party; no evidence links her to the Library
Parthenon converted to a three-aisled church of the Virgin Mary (Parthenos Maria, Theotokos) around the middle of the 6th century; later cathedral as Panagia Athiniotissa
13 May 609: Pope Boniface IV, with Emperor Phocas's permission, dedicated the Pantheon to Mary and all the martyrs; 28 carriages of martyrs' bones brought from Roman cemeteries
San Clemente, Rome: mithraeum built c.200 in an insula courtyard; 4th-century basilica over it, existing by 392 (Jerome); 12th-century basilica above; found in the 1860s by Joseph Mullooly

Malalas: emperor sent a decree to Athens 'ordering that no one should teach philosophy nor astrology' (undated, c.527-529); Codex law permits only the orthodox to teach and accept a public stipend; Agathias's story of seven philosophers incl. Damascius and Simplicius going to Persia and returning after 532 is single-source; Alan Cameron: possibly only funding cut; Alexandria's schools never formally suppressed
Watts (JRS 2004): Malalas 18.47 is the only direct ancient statement on the end of Athenian philosophical teaching; argues a local, narrow measure, unremarkable to contemporaries

Procopius Wars 1.19.36-37: Justinian decided to tear down the Philae sanctuaries; Narses 'tore down the sanctuaries at the emperor's order', put the priests under guard and 'sent the statues to Byzantium'
Philae: temple not actually destroyed; naos became church of St Stephen under Bishop Apa Theodore (6th c.) per inscription; last pagan graffiti c.457

Dijkstra: Procopius dates closure 535-537; thesis that Egyptian cults 'were already dying by themselves'; Isis festival attested into early 5th c., gone by mid-6th; priestly inscriptions thin out c.456/457

Library of Alexandria: Plutarch says Caesar's fire (48 BCE) burned the library, disputed; Bagnall thinks Aurelian's war in the 270s most probable occasion of large damage; Gibbon blamed the Serapeum 391; Arab-conquest bath story appears six centuries later, widely regarded as fiction; Bagnall: gradual neglect and decay

Eunapius, describing the Serapeum's destruction (Lives 472), says they 'imported monks, as they called them' into the sacred places and that 'every man who wore a black robe' had tyrannical power; the Alaric passage (476) speaks only of 'men clad in black raiment' and does not use the word monks

vt33_what_was_lost.topic: What was lost (Porphyry's book, mystery texts, Athenian school) and how the ascent teaching survived (Pseudo-Dionysius, Arabic Plotinus/Proclus, Ficino)

claims.text: Porphyry's Against the Christians: Theodosius II ordered every copy burned in 435 and again in 448; Constantine and other emperors banned and burned it (Digeser); no copy survives; known only from c.30 Christian refutations incl. Eusebius and Jerome

Pseudo-Dionysius wrote late 5th/early 6th c. under the name of Paul's convert; first clear citation Severus of Antioch 518-528; four treatises (Divine Names, Celestial Hierarchy, Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, Mystical Theology) and ten letters; triad purification-illumination-perfection; 'theurgy is the consummation of theology'; Eriugena translation 862; influenced Eckhart, Tauler, Cusanus, Cloud of Unknowing; Valla doubted 1457, Erasmus publicised from 1504

Proclus's influence: Pseudo-Dionysius drew heavily on him ('conquering Europe in the guise of an early Christian', Dodds); Liber de causis a 9th-c. Arabic adaptation of the Elements of Theology circulating under Aristotle's name, identified by Aquinas; Ficino followed Proclus; later Neoplatonists Damascius, Olympiodorus, Simplicius, Philoponus preserved fragments

Theology of Aristotle: 9th-century Arabic paraphrase of parts of Plotinus's Enneads, adapted by Ibn Na'ima al-Himsi (a Christian), edited by al-Kindi; falsely attributed to Aristotle; influenced al-Kindi and Avicenna (who wrote a commentary); Latin by Patricius, Ferrara 1591

Ficino finished his Latin translation of the Hermetic Pimander in 1463 from a Greek manuscript brought from Macedonia for Cosimo de' Medici; eight editions before 1500; then translated Plato and Dionysius the Areopagite
